title: His students
hook: Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani spread the school

segments.voice: Yesterday, ra'y, considered judgment, and your line: reasoned preference. When you chose between two good options, could you name the reason out loud? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-three.

In the classic Hanafi law books, a small, strange habit shows up again and again. A ruling is given, and then: Abu Hanifa said this, but Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said that. The founder of the school, contradicted by his own students, on the same page, in the school's own book. Nobody tore the page out. Nobody threw the students out. Their names sit beside his, and sometimes later Hanafi scholars even follow the students' view instead of the teacher's. That's an odd way to honor a teacher, until you see what the students were doing. Today: his students.
screen: `ABU HANIFA SAID THIS.` → `HIS STUDENTS SAID THAT.` → `ON THE SAME PAGE.`

segments.voice: The first is Abu Yusuf. He sat in Abu Hanifa's circle in Kufa, and later he served as a judge for the Abbasid caliphs. For the caliph Harun al-Rashid he wrote a book on taxes and the public treasury, Kitab al-Kharaj, giving the school's reasoning a place at court. The second is Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Shaybani, the great writer of the pair. His books set down the school's positions in order, and Hanafi scholars came to treat a set of them as the school's core record. Hanafi scholars say that much of Abu Hanifa's teaching reached later readers through what these two wrote. Next, the habit from the hook. Hanafi books call the three the imams of the school, and the students are called the two companions. When they disagreed with their teacher, they said so, and the books kept every view. For a school built on reasoned judgment, that fits. A student who repeats a teacher's answers carries the answers. A student who learned the method can carry the method, even past the teacher. Then this week, because today closes it. Most of life simply permitted. Ijtihad, the effort to understand. Taqlid, following one who knows. Difference as mercy. Abu Hanifa the merchant, and ra'y, judgment with a proof behind it. And now the people who made sure any of it survived. Last, the sentence under all of it. A school isn't one man. It's a teacher, and students honest enough to argue with him, and to write it all down.
screen: `ABU YUSUF: THE JUDGE AT COURT.` · `AL-SHAYBANI: THE WRITER.` · `THE TWO COMPANIONS DISAGREE ON THE PAGE.` · `A WEEK OF METHOD, CARRIED ON.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank a student who carried your work. Bring to mind someone who learned something from you. A younger sibling you taught to ride a bike. A new colleague you trained. A child who now does a recipe your way, or better than your way. Hold their face for a moment. Notice what they kept, and what they changed. If they disagree with you now on something, notice that too. Then decide on one short thank-you you could send today. If you pray, you can remember them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
His students. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani, the two companions, who wrote the Hanafi school down and spread it, keeping their own views beside their teacher's. Today's word.
Your line: students carry it. Today, send that thank-you to someone who learned from you, and tell them one thing they do better than you did. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Hanafi law books record the views of Abu Hanifa beside those of his students Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani, and later Hanafi jurists weigh all three when deciding the school's position.

fork.setup: you're a student of Abu Hanifa, and on one question you've reached a different answer than his. what does the school do with your view?
options: strike it out, out of respect for the teacher.
record it beside his, by name.
keep it secret until he dies.
fork.reveal: the books say Abu Hanifa held this, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad held that, and sometimes later jurists follow the students.

original.note: Arabic: students, pupils; the Hanafi books also call the two the sahiban, the two companions.

trapdoor: what you thought: a school is one founder's rulings, repeated.
what it means: a school is a method, carried and argued over by students who wrote it down.
what a scholar hears: the sahiban, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, and al-Shaybani's books treated as the school's core record.

sources.ref: Muhammad al-Shaybani, the books of zahir al-riwayah (e.g. al-Asl, al-Jami' al-Saghir)

notes: Abu Yusuf as judge (chief judge) under the Abbasids, and Kitab al-Kharaj written for Harun al-Rashid: confirm.
Al-Shaybani's books (zahir al-riwayah) as the school's core record: confirm framing; the script gives no count of the books.
'Much of what anyone knows of Abu Hanifa's teaching comes through what these two wrote': confirm this is a fair, unexaggerated statement.
'Later Hanafi scholars sometimes follow the students' view': confirm; the 'three imams' and 'the two companions' (sahiban) labels: confirm.
